failure_modes: Capture-reagent incompatibility or buffer effects reduce capture efficiency in specific formulations, causing false 'loss' calls even though EV membranes and cargo are intact (assay artifact).

Formulation excipients or device-shear release non-vesicular particles or protein aggregates that inflate particle counts and protein:particle ratios, obscuring true EV degradation (false 'preserved' calls).

Spike-in exogenous intact-EV tracer behaves differently from endogenous product EVs in given buffers or fractionation workflows, undermining its utility to detect assay interference or to normalize readouts.

Particle counters (NTA/TRPS) detect non-vesicular nanoparticles or label-artefacts; co-localization with capture fractions may reflect non-specific adsorption rather than bona fide surface-marker+ EVs.

Protected-cargo assays (targeted small-RNA, targeted proteomics) lack sensitivity or are differentially affected by detergents/excipients across conditions, producing inconsistent protection readouts across lots (unmeasurable or irreproducible fingerprints).

Insufficient conditioned-medium yield or lot-to-lot heterogeneity prevents n>=3 independent lots from being tested across the full matrix, reducing statistical confidence and enabling overinterpretation of stochastic assay variation.

Even if orthogonal in vitro signatures can be defined, they may not predict in vivo delivery or function because route- and species-specific clearance or nasal retention prevent brain delivery independent of product stability (translatability failure).
Labeling or fractionation steps introduce artifacts (e.g., reporter retention in nasal lavage as seen in NHP) that confound linking in vitro stability signatures to in vivo recovery or efficacy.
strongest_objection: The plan most likely fails or misleads because formulation excipients, fractionation buffers, or capture reagents will interfere with one or more orthogonal assays (immuno-capture, particle counting, protected-cargo profiling), producing apparent qualitative ‘loss’ or ‘preservation’ of EV-associated signals that reflect assay incompatibility or non-vesicular co-isolates rather than true membrane/cargo damage; if assay interference cannot be conclusively excluded by the proposed compatibility controls and spike-ins, the attributes will be unmeasurable or misleading for stability gating and comparability decisions.
